text: Renaissance (RE) is a political party in France described as liberal and centrist or centre-right. It was originally founded as En Marche! (EM) in April 2016 by Emmanuel Macron, a former Minister of the Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs, who was elected president in the 2017 presidential election with 66.1% of the second-round vote. The party later became known as La République En Marche! (LREM), LaREM, or REM, before officially adopting its current name, Renaissance, in September 2022. Established on 6 April 2016 in Amiens by Macron, aged 38, with the help of political advisor Ismaël Emelien, the party's name shares the same initials as Macron's name. The launch of En Marche! signaled Macron’s intention to run for president and served as a fundraising platform. The party was widely covered by the media and quickly gained traction in opinion polls, positioning Macron as a main competitor on the left. En Marche! recruited 4,000 volunteers to conduct door-to-door surveys of 100,000 people to develop a campaign closer to the electorate. Ludovic Chaker became the first general secretary and later deputy general secretary, overseeing campaign operations for the 2017 presidential election. La République En Marche! ran candidates in most constituencies, with at least half from civil society, half previously holding political office, and half being women; candidates could not run in more than one constituency. Prospective candidates had to demonstrate probity, political plurality, and efficacy, and those seeking endorsement had to sign up online, receiving nearly 15,000 applications. For political figures, the party considered popularity, establishment, and media skills, with some cases decided by Macron personally. Outgoing deputies from the Socialist Party (PS) or Republicans (LR) had to leave their parties to join LREM, though Macron waived this requirement on 5 May 2017, and later spokesperson Christophe Castaner stated that members could remain in the PS as long as they supported Macron. Civil society members could be mayors or regional councilors. After François Bayrou endorsed Macron, MoDem reserved 90 constituencies for its candidates, 50 of which were reported as winnable. On 15 May 2017, Édouard Philippe, a member of LR, was appointed Prime Minister. On 18 June 2017, LREM won an absolute majority in the National Assembly with 308 seats (53% of seats) after securing 43.06% of the vote in the second round, while MoDem secured 42 seats. In the 2017 Senate election, LREM lost seven seats, ending with 21, due to the indirect electoral system disadvantaging new parties. The first party congress was held in Lyon on 19 November 2017, where Christophe Castaner was elected leader by a council of 800, with a quarter being party members, for a three-year term. The event drew criticism, including a walk-out by 100 attendees citing lack of internal democracy and corruption. In Val-d'Oise's 1st constituency, a by-election was called after deputy Isabelle Muller-Quoy’s replacement, Michel Alexeef, was deemed ineligible. Muller-Quoy won the first round by 18 percentage points in 2017 but only by 5 in the by-election and lost to LR’s Antoine Savignat, marking the party’s first loss in the National Assembly. Subsequent by-elections showed a 10% swing against LREM. Ahead of the 2019 European Parliament election, LREM was expected to cooperate with ALDE, but due to domestic unrest and rising populism, Macron instead launched a pro-European campaign under the banner of Renaissance, leading to the formation of Renew Europe in June 2019, a centrist and liberal alliance that became the third-largest group in the European Parliament. For the 2020 municipal elections, LREM aimed to elect around 10,000 councillors, securing approximately 6,000 by the first round, mainly in small towns and rural areas, and investing 592 lead candidates in municipalities over 9,000 inhabitants, 289 of whom were official LREM members. The party forged 76 alliances with right-leaning and 33 with left-leaning lists in larger towns, partly due to the political landscape from 2014, though it preferred left alliances that declined to cooperate. Despite its ambitions, LREM failed to win any major city, claiming only 146 mayors in municipalities over 9,000 inhabitants and three in cities over 30,000, all won by right-wing incumbents supported by LREM. In symbolic cities like Paris and Lyon, candidates suffered heavy defeats, often finishing third or fourth. In Bordeaux, an alliance with a right-wing incumbent failed to block a surge by the ecologists, and a “green wave” led by EELV swept through major urban centers, dashing LREM’s hopes. Candidates often avoided displaying the party’s logo due to public dissatisfaction from the Yellow vests movement, pension reform protests, youth climate strikes, and pandemic handling. In May 2022, following Macron’s re-election, LREM announced a rebranding, with its parliamentary group adopting the name Renaissance to symbolize political renewal and reform. In September 2022, the party formally changed its name to Renaissance, establishing it as the new identity of the party itself. This rebranding aimed to consolidate Macron’s presidential majority into a single political force, aligning with his goal of transcending the traditional left-right divide. Two smaller parties, Agir and Territories of Progress, merged into Renaissance, but key allies like MoDem and Horizons retained independence within the Ensemble coalition. After a poor performance in the European Parliament elections, Macron dissolved the National Assembly on 9 June 2024, triggering snap elections on 30 June and 7 July 2024. Renaissance led the centrist Ensemble coalition, which included MoDem, Horizons, UDI, and the Radical Party, but internal tensions arose, especially with Horizons refusing to fully campaign under the Renaissance banner and demanding autonomy, leading to separate candidate declarations. Renaissance invested over 200 candidates, including ministers like Gabriel Attal and Gérald Darmanin, former ministers like Élisabeth Borne and Olivier Véran, and new faces such as Stéphane Séjourné and Loïc Signor. In the first round on 30 June, the Ensemble coalition received only about 21% of the vote, behind the Rassemblement National (33.1%) and the left-wing Nouveau Front Populaire (28%), with only four candidates elected outright and Renaissance leading in just 70 constituencies before the run-off. In the second round on 7 July 2024, no bloc achieved a majority; the Nouveau Front Populaire became the largest with approximately 182 seats, followed by Ensemble with about 163, and the Rassemblement National with about 143. Renaissance’s seat count dropped from 245 in 2022 to about 160–162. This outcome triggered a political crisis within the centrist bloc, prompting Prime Minister Gabriel Attal to convene an emergency meeting and later be elected president of the Renaissance group in the National Assembly on 13 July. Discussions continued over a possible alliance between Renaissance and the Republicans (LR) to form a working majority, though such a coalition would still fall short of the 289 seats needed for an absolute majority. Although Macron was a member of the PS from 2006 to 2009 and independent from 2009 to 2016, La République En Marche! seeks to transcend traditional political boundaries as a transpartisan organization. The party has been described as centrist, centre-right, or big tent, with some sources labeling it as centre-left in 2019; Macron described it in 2016 as a progressive party uniting left and right. It is culturally and socially liberal, and economically liberal, and has been described as using anti-establishment, populist strategies comparable to the UK Labour Party’s Third Way. An Ipsos survey in March 2018 found that public perception of the party had shifted rightward, with 45% classifying it as centre-right (25%) to right-wing (20%), down from 33% in March 2017, while 21% placed it in the centre. The party considers anyone who submits identification information (date of birth, email, full address, telephone number) and adheres to its charter as a member, and unlike other parties, does not require a monetary donation. Macron has stated it is possible to join LREM while remaining a member of another republican party. On 10 April 2016, Macron claimed 13,000 members, but Le Canard enchaîné accused him of inflating the figure, noting it was actually the number of website clicks. Ismaël Emelien clarified that each member signs a charter of values and has a voice in the general assembly, distinguishing it from newsletter sign-ups.

In 2017, La République En Marche! considers every individual who provides identification information—such as date of birth, email, full address, and telephone number—and adheres to the party's charter as a member. Unlike other political parties, it does not require members to make a monetary donation. Macron stated that it is possible to join La République En Marche! while remaining a member of another republican party. On 10 April 2016, shortly after the movement's launch, Macron claimed 13,000 members, but Le Canard enchaîné accused him of inflating the figure, asserting that 13,000 represented website clicks rather than actual members. Ismaël Emelien, Macron's advisor, clarified that each member signs a charter of values and has a voice in the movement's general assembly, distinguishing this from those who only subscribe to the newsletter, who are in greater number. Sylvain Fort confirmed that the movement verifies email addresses but acknowledged that the system depends on the honesty of members. In October 2016, Macron stated that En Marche! was "neck and neck with the Socialist Party" in membership after seven months, according to Mediapart, which noted that the membership included many independents and executives but few functionaries, farmers, or unemployed individuals, and that many members had never been politically engaged, having only left their information on the party website. The movement draws inspiration from the participatory model of Désirs d'avenir, Ségolène Royal's movement, and intends to rely on its member files, as noted by deputy Pascal Terrasse and former leader of Désirs d'avenir. According to Libération, the movement uses a pyramidal enrolment system inspired by Barack Obama's 2008 and 2012 campaigns. Through its participatory model, each adherent can freely join or create a local committee, which is led by one or more adherents who organize local events, meetings, and debates centered on the movement's values. By December 2016, La République En Marche! had over 2,600 such committees. Christian Dargnat, former general director of BNP Paribas Asset Management, leads the party's financial association, which has raised funds since its creation. In 2016, Georges Fenech, a Republican deputy, alerted the National Assembly that the association continued fundraising during Macron's trip to London, prompting Prime Minister Manuel Valls to issue an official denial despite prior statements from En Marche!. Macron declared in May 2016 that 2,000 donors had contributed financially to the party, and by December 2016, he reported over 10,000 donors contributing between 1 euro and 7,500 euros. By the end of December 2016, the party had collected between 4 and 5 million euros in donations. By the end of March, this amount exceeded 9 million euros from 35,000 donations, averaging 257 euros per donation, with 600 donors contributing half of the total, including those giving over 5,000 euros. In the book Dans l'enfer de Bercy: Enquête sur les secrets du ministère des Finances (JC Lattès, 2017) by Frédéric Says and Marion L'Hour, Macron was accused of using 120,000 euros from the state budget between 1 January and 30 August 2016 to fund his presidential campaign. In the European Parliament, La République En Marche! sits in the Renew Europe group with five MEPs. In the European Committee of the Regions, the party is part of the Renew Europe CoR group for the 2025–2030 mandate, with three full members and one alternate member. Anne Rudisuhli is Coordinator in the SEDEC Commission and Magali Altounian is Chair of the CIVEX Commission and a member of the Bureau of the Renew Europe CoR Group.
